content.intro: Learn exact and approximate numeric types in the context of mysql data types. This lesson covers the supplied syllabus topic, demonstrates a representative MySQL example, and finishes with a verification task.
content.why_it_matters: A column type defines which values can be represented and affects precision, storage, comparison, and conversion. Choose a type from real domain rules; do not rely on accidental coercion or approximate numeric types for exact money values.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Choose a type for a realistic value, then explain its valid range, precision, nullability and conversion behavior. Write down the expected result before running the snippet. Compare actual output with the reference, then try one normal case and one edge case.

content_blocks.code: SELECT CAST(120 AS SIGNED) AS quantity, CAST(19.95 AS DECIMAL(6,2)) AS price, CAST(1 AS UNSIGNED) AS active_flag;
content_blocks.expected_output: One row returns an integer, exact decimal value, and unsigned value.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a sample result proves the whole design is correct.
common_mistakes.why: Edge cases such as NULLs, duplicate matches, concurrency, privileges, or version differences may change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a targeted boundary case and record the server version, schema and expected result.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a mutating or administrative example in the wrong environment.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data changes, access grants, and recovery commands may have persistent impact.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable lab, preview targets and permissions, and write a reset/recovery plan before executing.
